claims.claim: Economic development refers to how and why material prosperity varies across places and how that variation is measured; the most common economic measures are GDP per capita and gross national income (GNI) per capita.

The World Bank sorts economies into four income groups by GNI per capita; for its 2027 fiscal year (based on 2025 GNI, Atlas method, in US dollars) the thresholds are: low income $1,175 or less; lower-middle income $1,176 to $4,635; upper-middle income $4,636 to $14,375; high income more than $14,375.

The World Bank converts national income to comparable US dollars using the Atlas method, which averages exchange rates over the current and prior two years and adjusts for inflation to smooth short-term currency swings.

The Human Development Index (HDI), published by the UN Development Programme, is a composite that combines three dimensions: a long and healthy life (life expectancy at birth), knowledge (expected years of schooling and mean years of schooling), and a decent standard of living (GNI per capita, PPP).

The three HDI dimension indices are each normalized to a 0-to-1 scale and then combined using their geometric mean, giving an overall HDI value between 0 and 1, where higher means greater human development.

The categories 'developed' and 'developing' are imprecise because they group together economies that differ enormously; the World Bank stopped drawing a firm developed/developing line in its main data publication in 2016 in favor of the income-group classification.

Income groups themselves hide internal variation: a high-income country can contain large numbers of people in poverty or high inequality, and many of the world's poorest people live in countries classified as middle-income.

Geographers describe the world economy with a core-periphery structure: a wealthy, industrialized, technology-intensive core and a lower-income periphery that supplies raw materials and labor, with an intermediate semi-periphery in Wallerstein's version.

Modernization theory, associated with W. W. Rostow's 1960 book 'The Stages of Economic Growth', argues that countries pass through a similar linear sequence of five stages (traditional society, preconditions for take-off, take-off, drive to maturity, high mass consumption) as they industrialize.

Dependency theory (associated with Andre Gunder Frank) and Immanuel Wallerstein's world-systems analysis (1974) offer a competing view: they locate poverty in the structure of the global economy, arguing that wealth flows from periphery to core so that core prosperity and peripheral poverty are linked.

The UN's 17 Sustainable Development Goals were adopted by all member states in 2015 as part of the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development, a shared framework with a target year of 2030 covering goals such as ending poverty, quality education, gender equality, and climate action.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Which theory correctly explains why prosperity varies across places
positions: Modernization theory (Rostow, 1960) holds that development is a broadly common sequence of stages and that poorer countries can follow the path richer ones took.
Dependency theory (Frank) and world-systems analysis (Wallerstein, 1974) hold that global economic structure keeps peripheral regions poor by channeling wealth to the core.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: Presented neutrally as two competing schools of thought, attributed to their originators, without endorsing either. The lesson notes both are influential frameworks and that neither is a settled fact.

positions: The terms remain in wide everyday and institutional use as a rough shorthand.
Critics, including the World Bank's own statisticians, say the binary is too imprecise to be analytically useful and prefer income groups.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson keeps the terms because students will meet them, but flags their imprecision and presents the income-group classification as the more precise alternative.

unsupportedExistingClaims: The generated draft was generic boilerplate ('Economic Development is a foundational concept students use to organize information') with no measures, theories, or data; none of it was usable as evidence.
correctionsNeeded: Replaced boilerplate with the actual content: measures (GDP/GNI per capita, income groups, HDI), the developed/developing imprecision, core-periphery, the modernization-vs-dependency debate, and the SDGs.
Added dated, attributed figures (World Bank FY2027 income thresholds based on 2025 GNI; HDI methodology from the UNDP 2023/24 technical notes; SDGs adopted 2015, target 2030).
Added neutral, attributed presentation of the theory debate as required by the subject source-map, endorsing neither school.

sourceRecords.title: Human Development Report 2023/24 Technical Notes: Calculating the human development indices
sourceRecords.provider: United Nations Development Programme (Human Development Report Office)
sourceRecords.notes: Read via the companion HDRO training PDF (hditraining.pdf) and this technical-note PDF. Supports the three HDI dimensions and their indicators (Health = life expectancy at birth; Education = expected years of schooling and mean years of schooling; Standard of living = GNI per capita), the normalization of each indicator to a 0-1 dimension index (e.g., life expectancy min 20, max 85), and that the HDI is the geometric mean of the three dimension indices. Facts restated in original prose; no wording reproduced.

sourceRecords.notes: Supports the plain-language summary of the HDI as a summary composite of achievement in three key dimensions of human development - a long and healthy life, knowledge, and a decent standard of living - published by UNDP. Used only to name and briefly describe HDI; depth is deferred to the human-development-indicators topic. Reference-only.

sourceRecords.title: World Bank Country and Lending Groups (income classifications)
sourceRecords.notes: Supports the four income groups and the fiscal-year-2027 GNI-per-capita thresholds (low income <= $1,175; lower-middle $1,176-$4,635; upper-middle $4,636-$14,375; high income > $14,375), based on 2025 GNI using the Atlas method in US dollars, and that thresholds are updated annually. Figures dated and attributed. Reference-only; facts restated.

sourceRecords.title: How does the World Bank classify countries by income?
sourceRecords.provider: Our World in Data (Joe Hasell and others)
sourceRecords.notes: Supports the four income groups and the Atlas method (averaging exchange rates over the current and prior two years, inflation-adjusted), and the imprecision point: high-income countries can still contain poverty and inequality, and many of the world's poorest people live in middle-income countries. Also supports the shift toward income-based classification over a developed/developing binary. CC BY 4.0; facts synthesized in original prose, no charts reproduced.
